en: Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhìràn of the Tang Dynasty.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Prediction of the Five Hundred Disciples":
since five hundred is first specified as the number, the character "receive" (shòu) must be employed. That "five hundred is a number" and so forth is not essential.
The section beginning with “The upper two cycles” is the question;
the section beginning with “The upper serves as” is the answer.

These likewise possess the four *siddhāntas*: first, the *loka-siddhānta*, because the three grades differ; second, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, because it removes aversion through the subsequent response; third, the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta*, because it causes people to produce great goodness through silent contemplation; and fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, because the ultimate principle of provisional and real teachings transcends words and thought.
The passage beginning with "What was the intention above? serves only to resolve doubts and does not constitute the four *siddhāntas*.

The section beginning with "We [have been unable to] comprehend the Buddha" describes the failure to fully grasp the teaching; having heard the parable for those of middling and superior faculties, they have comprehended the five periods and the stage of the *dharmakāya*, yet while they perceived the *upāya* within the interim, they saw only the *vairocana-kāya* (the exalted response body), and even the Tathāgata still rebuked them for what they had failed to comprehend.

Now that we have heard this, though we wish to grasp its meaning, how could we surpass the four great disciples? One should know that beyond what has been comprehended, there is much more that remains ungrasped; therefore, it is also said, "that which cannot be proclaimed."

However, having heard that Kāśyapa and Śāriputra fully received [the teachings], it is clear that the Tathāgata’s detailed exposition was not entirely obscure in its meaning; yet, admiring the loftiness and profundity of the Buddha-dharma, I have not dared to surpass their prior realization.

Regarding the phrase "assisting in the proclamation of my Dharma" and so forth: if one considers the fundamental [teaching] in light of its provisional manifestations, how could it be that he has not already assisted in the past under various Buddhas—whether in the *ekāyana* (single-vehicle) or *ardha-pūrṇa* (half-full) teachings, or the *pūrṇa* (full) teachings? It must be understood that within the full teachings, there are necessarily the inclusion of mutual aspects as well as the opening [of the gates].

Regarding the present Buddha’s appearance in this world of five turbidities, it is appropriate to employ teachings such as the provisional opening of the path and the sublation of the assembly; therefore, all [teachings] are expounded by way of analogy with similar cases. For instance, when Mañjuśrī cited the past light illuminating the eastern direction, was there not another path? This is merely an example of citing what is similar.

Regarding the passage from “having personally relinquished” to “is the skillful means”: if we base this on the statement excluding only the Buddha, then even those in the position of a successor (the *kṣetra-parigraha*) should be unfathomable. Since they are unfathomable, their fundamental and manifest aspects (*honjaku*) are difficult to measure. Not only did they [serve] under past Buddhas in the past, but their fundamental reality may also be equal to that of past Buddhas; since the fundamental reality of past Buddhas is itself difficult to measure, they might even be teachers of past Buddhas—not merely equal to them.
Regarding the term "seven expedient means" (saptopāya), this is merely discussed by contrasting the partial and the perfect.
Thus, one should know that the remote origin is profoundly obscure and difficult to fathom; if this is so, then this [teaching] is but the "origin within the traces."
The six *pāramitās* mutually encompass one another, as is fully explained in the second commentary on the *Zhi guan*.
The "Pūrṇa Chapter" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* describes how the six perfections mutually adorn one another.
Regarding the phrase "as can be understood from the text," the characteristics of the sūtra’s wording correspond clearly to their respective meanings.

Furthermore, although the five periods of teaching listed in various texts are purely paths of goodness, there are still differences in quality within them. For instance, if there were no women, there would certainly be no evil realms; or at times, even when women are present, there may be no evil realms—as in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, where women exist but the affairs of women do not, or in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where both are absent. These differing characteristics cannot be listed in full detail; however, one may roughly infer them by understanding how the three grades of each—both in terms of the Vehicle (the teaching) and the Precepts (the practice)—interweave with one another.
Regarding the phrase "The Ninth Dharma-Food of the Moon-Treasury Sūtra" and so forth: "Dharma-food" refers to hearing the Dharma.
For example, those born of the lower grade in the realm of Sukhāvatī constantly hear Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara preaching the Dharma while within their lotus flowers.

Regarding "the food of the joy of Dharma": this refers to rejoicing upon hearing the Dharma; while the act of hearing properly belongs to the food of Dharma, having heard it constitutes the food of joy.
Regarding "the food of dhyāna": this means sustaining oneself through the methods of dhyāna without requiring material food; alternatively, the Dharma itself may be the joy.

The fifth fascicle of the *Candragarbha-sūtra* describes ten merits for each of the ten wholesome actions; this is also identical in intent to the passage in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* concerning the ten wholesome actions as the pure land of a bodhisattva. Therefore, at the end of each item, it states that one will subsequently become a Buddha, and so forth.
The fifth sutra, the "Chapter on Faith and Reverence," states:
"The purity and equality of the precepts consist of the cessation of the ten paths of unwholesome action. By ceasing the taking of life, one attains ten merits."

What are the ten? First, one attains fearlessness toward all sentient beings; second, one attains a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings; third, one severs evil habitual karma; fourth, one is free from illness and possesses decisive resolve; fifth, one enjoys a long life; sixth, one is protected by non-human beings; seventh, one has no evil dreams; eighth, one has no enemies; ninth, one does not fear the evil realms; and tenth, at the end of life, one is reborn in a good realm.

If one can use this breath to extinguish the roots of goodness and dedicate them toward Bodhi, one will certainly reach Bodhi and attain unsurpassed wisdom; when reaching Bodhi, that realm will be free from all harm and weapons, and long-lived beings will be reborn in that land.
The nine [sections] below and the tenth are identical from the point where it says, "If one can... and so forth.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva practices non-killing during the causal stage as a cause for a pure land, by fulfilling the four dharmas—such as not killing oneself and teaching others not to kill—when he later attains Buddhahood, beings of ten classes will be born together in that land.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states:

"The ten wholesome paths are the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings whose lives are not cut short prematurely and so forth will come to be born in that land."
Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is stated that when a bodhisattva practices a single path, all four dharmas must be present for it to become a pure cause.
Details regarding "Śāriputra manifesting anger" and so forth are fully cited as they appear in the second fascicle of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).

The primary intent of the text is to address ordinary people and non-Buddhists; therefore, it speaks of "the three poisons and false views. However, because this also incidentally serves the dual purpose of illustrating the practices of the Hīnayāna and demonstrating the universal [Mahāyāna] meaning, these points are further elaborated upon.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (云云): it means that one should fully cite the specific events and enumerate the practices, while also including the various partial indications given by each of the noble ones (*ārya*).
As for "Ājñātakauṇḍinya" and the others:
Question—If they are recorded separately at the beginning, why are they not recorded during the first week?
Answer:

Regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, the two initial stages differ; the two intentions for guiding beings toward aspiration are each distinct, and the methods employed in manifesting traces cannot be standardized.

From "The parables are twofold" up to "revealing the reality," all refer to those who receive the teaching through parables; therefore, the initial opening of the parables in the main text directly constitutes the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real. This corresponds to the passages where the three assemblies, the *śraddhādhimukta*, and the five hundred [arhats] receive their respective understandings—the intent of the textual structure of these three sections lies herein.
Regarding the statement, "For example, there are people who are those of the Two Vehicles," this refers to the capacities of the Two Vehicles.
For those of small capacity, at the time when [the realization] arises, it is still vast.

There are two meanings to "intoxication," which are identical in intent to the two meanings previously mentioned regarding "falling back. The first is the analogy for being childish and attached to the five desires; however, as in the case of Dharma Masters such as Sadāparibhūta, one may establish a karmic connection through even a single phrase. The second refers to those who are weak in goodness, or those at the initial stage of the Five Ranks who have not yet entered the stage of semblance; therefore, they are described as "weak."

Because the thickness of karmic connections varies, ignorance is accordingly designated as either light or heavy; thus it is said, "There are two kinds of intoxication. One should know that the poor person was originally intoxicated first, like one who receives fine delicacies and falls asleep after eating them. The auxiliary paths of the Three Teachings are like these delicacies, further employing diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the primary meaning.

Once the delicacies and meals have been digested, they are like expedient teachings that do not provide ultimate benefit. In the past, at the place of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, before the great connection was yet established, he encountered various flavors and heard all three teachings; even upon reaching the Lotus Sūtra, although he heard the Perfect and Sudden teaching, it merely served to establish a karmic connection, like tying a jewel to one's garment.

From "priceless" up to "the jewel of the wisdom of *tathatā*," this is explained according to the teaching (*śāsana*). Here, the cause of penetration (*prativedha-hetu*) is taken as the fastening of the jewel.
Because the teaching elucidates principle (*tattva*), it is called "*tathatā*"; because the teaching is the functional application of wisdom, it is called the "jewel of wisdom."
Regarding those who are to be transformed, the teaching that can generate wisdom is itself called "wisdom. The "jewel" has two meanings, both of which are treasures for the house of wisdom.

"Tying it inside his garment" means that at the time of first forming a karmic connection, one is endowed with the two garments; because they possess a sense of shame and dread of blame (*hrī-apatrāpya*) and have faith and joy, they are able to form a karmic connection.

If one regresses from the Mahāyāna and falls into evil states, they will lack the outer garment; if, in the present, they lack faith and joy, it would seem as though the inner garment is also absent. However, based on what was tied at that time, the internal seed still exists together with the original faith, so in meaning it is like the inner garment still being there. It is merely that the garment is worn out rather than being entirely without clothing; therefore, when a close friend points to the jewel inside the garment, it signifies pointing back to the time of the original sense of shame and faith.
According to this, there is no logical inconsistency in the fact that they are not clothed upon their bodies.

As for the passage from "having risen, they wander about" to "seeking the clothing and food of the Lesser Vehicle," they ought instead to seek precious garments and celestial delicacies; yet, because they have gone to other lands, they seek only such clothing as barely covers the body and such inferior food as merely sustains the frame.

In this passage, both interpretations of the other’s meaning are established; however, as for the pursuit of existence, it has become somewhat urgent today, which is why it says “weary of suffering,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “if one compares the Māra and the Buddha,” etc., since we have today first attained the “other” of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), we speak here by way of the Great and Small Vehicles. Thus we know that if one goes to another land seeking salvation, not only will food and clothing be insufficient, but one will also lose the treasure to which one is bound, because the friend who showed the jewel resides in one’s own native land.

Regarding the phrase "the intention of encouraging trade as a metaphor for receiving the prediction of Buddhahood": although a pearl may be worth countless treasures, it must be traded before its utility can be realized. Although the internal understanding of the *liǎoyīn* (the cause of completion) is ultimately perfected, one must necessarily exchange the latent for the manifest; that is, one exchanges the ancient principle of "understanding all through one" for the practice of "practicing all through one. The essence of the pearl is inexhaustible and the process of trade is likewise infinite; therefore, one must continue to listen and continue to cultivate in order to manifest the functional power of the treasure.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, once one obtains a maṇi jewel, it must undergo ten kinds of polishing before it can rain down treasures; likewise, only when one's understanding and practice correspond can one receive the Buddha’s prediction. From this point onward, one possesses the robe of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*), the food of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and the immeasurable treasures of self-cultivation and the transformation of others; in this stage of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), both self and others are inexhaustible.

Regarding the statement, "All three cycles contain this same intent": if one compares the "Exposition of the Dharma" (the first cycle) with the two subsequent cycles, the former is situated solely at the Bodhi tree. This is because when the Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree contemplating the time to employ the Great [Vehicle], he had not yet discussed the past during that Exposition of the Dharma.
Furthermore, according to the extant text, even within the parable of the second cycle—which mentions twenty trillion Buddhas—he likewise did not discuss the realms of atoms (reṇu-bindu).
However, did not those in the middle and upper assemblies also once tie the jewel at the place of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū?
Just as one who probes the collar finds the main collar, they have realized the Dharma-body; how could this have occurred merely under the Bodhi tree?
This is merely based on the extant text.

It is simply because [the disciples] possessed sharp faculties and attained faith and understanding immediately upon hearing [the teaching], without requiring a reference to the past; therefore, it was not discussed.
Thus, in the preceding passage, the initial engagement with the study of the Hīnayāna is taken as the intermediate stage; hence, it does not refer exclusively to the time at the Bodhi Tree.
The phrase "in such-and-such a year" and so forth applies only to the [first] impure [kalpa] and does not extend to the two subsequent cycles.

Regarding "the immeasurable Jewel of the Buddha": because a jewel is obtained through trade, it may also be called "the jewel obtained from the Buddha," which refers to the benefiting of others (parārtha).

Regarding the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Learners and Non-learners": the introductory text of this chapter should fully comprise the four *siddhāntas*. The distinction between learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) corresponds to the worldly level (*loka-saṃvṛti*); the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) corresponds to the level for individuals (*puruṣakāra*); the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) corresponds to the level of remediation (*pratipakṣa*); and the stage of non-learning corresponds to the ultimate level (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, "attaining the prediction" (vyākaraṇa) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the classification by teaching (*yàojiào*), the three teachings are as stated in the text; the phrase "investigating the Tathāgatagarbha" excludes the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).

Moreover, as explained in the General Preface (*tōngxù*) concerning the contemplation of the mind (*guānxīn*): among the six stages of identity (*liùjí*), the stage of ultimate identity constitutes the stage of no-more-learning (*wúxuéwèi*); the remaining four are termed stages of learning (*xué*); and the stage of principle-identity (*lǐjí*) is neither learning nor no-more-learning.

Furthermore, regarding the "six identities" (*liù jí*): in their general sense, they are all neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naśaikṣa-na-aśaikṣa*); from the stage of partial realization (*fēnzhēn*) onward, however, they are both learner (*śaikṣa*) and non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
The phrase "and so forth" refers to what was briefly mentioned above.

Regarding the phrase "the two are among those numbered above": although they are listed among those of great learning (*bahuśruta*), why are those who have now received their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) included here?

In the answer, it is argued that while their attainment of the prediction is discussed in general, they remain within the assembly of twelve hundred and are still the superior stream among those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
Although it is recognized by many people, this is intended to guide those of inferior faculties.

If that is so, you have not answered the previous question; since the intent of the question was no different from the previous one, why does the current answer merely state "the superior among the middling-inferior"? How can this be considered an answer?
However, it is not the ultimate [teaching], because it is intended to lead toward the reality [of the truth] and because of the four *siddhāntas*.
(Fahua Wenzuji, Scroll 8, Part 2)
